blocks.prompt: The Caterpillar That Rebuilds Itself
blocks.text: A caterpillar hatches from an egg. The egg is smaller than a grain of rice. The caterpillar's first job is to eat. It eats and eats and eats. In two weeks it can grow thousands of times heavier than when it hatched. A caterpillar has six real legs at the front. It has soft stubby legs at the back. Those soft legs have tiny hooks on them. The hooks grab the leaf and hold on tight. That is why a caterpillar can walk upside down under a branch and never fall.

3.title: The Caterpillar That Rebuilds Itself
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then answer the questions.

notes: Six real legs, plus soft stumps called prolegs

blocks.prompt: A Body Built for Eating
blocks.text: Look closely at a caterpillar and you will find a body built for one job. Up front are six real legs. Those are the same six legs it will keep when it is a butterfly. Behind them are fat little stumps called prolegs. Prolegs are not real legs at all. They are soft, and the bottom of each one is covered in tiny hooks. Those hooks grip a leaf so well that a caterpillar can hang under a branch in the wind and stay put. A caterpillar has no nose and no lungs. It breathes through a row of small holes along its sides. The holes are called spiracles. Air goes in through them and travels around the body in tiny tubes. It also has a problem. A caterpillar's skin is stiff and does not stretch much, but the caterpillar keeps growing. So every few days it splits the old skin down the back and crawls out of it. Underneath is a new, roomier skin that has been waiting all along. Most caterpillars do this four or five times before they finish growing. The old skin is left behind on the leaf, empty, still shaped like the animal that walked out of it.

4.title: The Caterpillar That Rebuilds Itself
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A caterpillar is a larva: the feeding stage
Twelve simple eyes, and still nearly blind
Silk comes out of a nozzle below the jaws
Each stage between molts is an instar
Monarchs store milkweed poison in their bodies
Bold bands are a warning, not decoration

blocks.prompt: The Eating Stage
blocks.text: Every caterpillar is a larva, which is the young feeding stage of a butterfly or a moth. Its whole design points at one task. The head is a hard capsule carrying a pair of jaws that work sideways, like scissors, chewing through leaf after leaf. Just below the jaws is a spinneret, a nozzle that squeezes out liquid silk. The silk hardens the moment it meets the air. A caterpillar lays a silk trail wherever it goes and grips that trail with its hooked prolegs, which is a large part of why it does not fall. You might expect an animal that hunts for leaves all day to have good eyes. It does not. On each side of its head sit six tiny simple eyes called stemmata. All twelve together can tell light from dark and not much more. A caterpillar finds its meal mostly by touch and by smell, tapping the world with a pair of short antennae. Growth is the whole point, and growth is also the whole problem. A caterpillar's outer skin is stiff and cannot stretch far. So the caterpillar eats until that skin is painfully tight, splits it, and climbs out wearing a larger one that formed underneath. Each stage between molts is called an instar. Most caterpillars pass through five instars in a few weeks and finish thousands of times heavier than the speck that hatched from the egg. Monarch caterpillars go one step further. They feed only on milkweed, a plant that carries bitter chemicals strong enough to make a bird sick. Instead of breaking those chemicals down, the caterpillar stores them in its own body. Its bold yellow, black, and white bands are not decoration. They are a warning, and birds learn to read it.

5.title: The Caterpillar That Rebuilds Itself
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Butterflies make a chrysalis, moths usually spin a cocoon
Enzymes dissolve most of the caterpillar's tissue
Imaginal discs are carried from the day it hatches
One disc per wing, leg, eye, and antenna
Parts of the nervous system survive the rebuild
Metamorphosis is Greek for a change of shape

blocks.prompt: Eating Yourself Into Something Else
blocks.text: The caterpillar's last act is the strangest thing it does. After weeks of nothing but eating and molting, something changes. The caterpillar stops feeding, empties its gut, and wanders away from the plant that fed it. A monarch spins a small button of silk on the underside of a leaf, grips the button with a hook at its tail, and hangs upside down in the shape of the letter J. Then it molts one final time. The skin peels back, and what emerges is not a bigger caterpillar. It is a chrysalis: a smooth, sealed case with no legs, no jaws, and no way to eat. People often say the caterpillar turns to soup inside. That is close to true, and it badly undersells what is happening. Most of the caterpillar's tissue really does break down. Enzymes dissolve muscle and gut into a thick broth of raw material. But the broth is not the story. Since the day it hatched, the caterpillar has carried small folded clusters of cells called imaginal discs, tucked away and doing nothing at all. There is a disc for each wing, for each leg, for the eyes, for the antennae. Inside the chrysalis those discs finally switch on. They feed on the dissolved caterpillar and build the butterfly out of it. The animal is quite literally consuming itself in order to construct its own replacement. Not everything melts. Much of the nervous system carries through, which raises an obvious question: does the butterfly remember being a caterpillar? In 2008, a research team at Georgetown University trained tobacco hornworm caterpillars to avoid one particular smell. Weeks later, the moths those caterpillars had become still avoided it. Something had crossed the gap. This is why the word for what happens here is not growth. It is metamorphosis, from Greek words meaning a change of shape. Growing is what the caterpillar did for weeks on the leaf. Rebuilding a new animal out of its own dissolved body is something else entirely.

6.title: The Caterpillar That Rebuilds Itself
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Order Lepidoptera: butterflies and moths
Pupa is the stage between larva and adult
Imaginal discs are present before hatching
The nervous system is remodeled, not destroyed
Blackiston, Casey and Weiss, 2008: memory survives
Some monarchs fly thousands of kilometers

blocks.prompt: The Caterpillar's Last Trick
blocks.text: Consider a problem in engineering. You have built a machine that is very good at exactly one job: eating. It is a soft tube with jaws at one end, six real legs, ten gripping stumps, and a brain the size of a pinhead. Now convert it into a machine that does a completely different job. The new machine must fly, drink nectar through a coiled straw, see in color, find a mate, and, if it is a monarch, travel thousands of kilometers to a mountain forest it has never seen. You may not throw the first machine away, because the material inside it is all you have. And you must do the whole conversion sealed inside a case, out in the open, with no help and no spare parts. That is metamorphosis, and it is the most extreme rebuild any animal attempts. The caterpillar prepares carefully. It stops feeding, empties its gut, and leaves the plant that has kept it alive. It spins a pad of silk, hooks itself in, hangs, and molts one final time. What comes out of that last skin is a pupa, called a chrysalis in butterflies and usually wrapped in a spun cocoon in moths. It has no legs and no mouth. From the outside, for a week or two, nothing happens. Inside, almost everything happens. Enzymes flood the body and digest the caterpillar's own tissue. Muscle, gut, and skin break down into a nutrient broth. This is the part everyone repeats, and it is where most retellings stop, which is a shame, because dissolving is the easy half. The hard half is whatever does the building. Since before it hatched, the caterpillar has carried tiny folded packets of cells called imaginal discs. There is one for each wing, one for each leg, one for each eye, one for the antennae. Through all those weeks of chewing they sat inactive, costing the animal almost nothing. In the pupa they switch on, draw on the broth of the dissolved caterpillar, and construct the adult out of it. The butterfly is not born from the caterpillar. It is built out of the caterpillar, the way a house can be built from the timber of the house that stood there before. Not everything is torn down. Much of the nervous system is remodeled rather than destroyed, and that leaves an uncomfortable question sitting in the open. If parts of the brain survive, does anything the caterpillar knew survive with them? In 2008, researchers at Georgetown University tested precisely that. They exposed tobacco hornworm caterpillars to a specific odor paired with a mild electric shock, and the caterpillars learned to avoid the smell. Those caterpillars then pupated, dissolved, and rebuilt themselves into moths. When the moths were offered the same odor, they avoided it too. Something had crossed the gap. An animal with a substantially reconstructed body had carried a memory through its own liquefaction. This is worth sitting with. We usually treat a life as one continuous thing: one body, slowly changing, from start to finish. The caterpillar does not fit that picture. It is a single animal that spends part of its life as one organism and part as an almost entirely different one, and the bridge between them is a stretch of time in which it is neither, dissolved into its own raw material, waiting on a set of cells it has carried since before it hatched to decide what it becomes next.
